name: Dull Opaline Green
lede: Dull Opaline Green is a very pale, slightly grayed green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, closer to celadon porcelain than to any garden green.

sections.title: A pale plate reference from 1912
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* plots this color on plate XIX at hue 37′, tone f, among its lightest green swatches [1]. As with the rest of that atlas, the published scan is an aged plate and only an approximation of Ridgway's original pigment [1]. Our own classification places it in the ISCC-NBS region called very pale green, Munsell notation 1.8G 8.8/2.0 [2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[pale-blue-green]], [[microcline-green]], [[lichen-green]] and [[pale-niagara-green]], at 3.3, 3.6, 3.8 and 5.1 ΔE [2]. Both readings agree: this is a green pulled toward blue and almost all the way to white, distinct from a saturated [[green]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this one covers at least five percent of the canvas in 38 paintings, about 0.2 percent overall, as photographed [3]. Nearly all of those appearances are highlights rather than shadows or mid-tones, which fits a near-white green [3]. Use is highest in the 1860s, more than five times the archive's average rate for that decade, and the color's single strongest companion word is Celadon, at over two hundred times its average co-occurrence [3]. These counts come from photographs of varnished paintings, not from pigment analysis [3].
